newsitem.title: FRANCE: Court awards Tapie liquidators 600 million francs.
newsitem.headline: Court awards Tapie liquidators 600 million francs.

text.p: A Paris court on Thursday ordered a former unit of ailing state bank Credit Lyonnais to pay a provisional 600 million francs ($120 million) for lending businessman Bernard Tapie too much money and contributing to his downfall.

The commercial court awarded the sum to the liquidators of Tapie's industrial empire who filed suit last June against Credit Lyonnais and its former units SDBO and Clinvest, alleging they provided "excessive support" to Tapie.
The ex-politician and former boss of Marseille European soccer champions is now bankrupt and is appealing against prison sentences for match-rigging and business fraud.
Societe de Banque Occidentale (SDBO) -- best known as Tapie's banker in the 1980s -- "took excessive and conscious risks," the court ruled on Thursday.
It "knew from 1989 the two main companies belonging to Tapie, GBT (Groupe Bernard Tapie) and FIBT (Financiere et immobiliere Bernard Tapie) were in a state of default," it said.
"Not only did SDBO maintain its assistance but it increased it, creating an insurmountable debt," the court said.

Tapie, who owes Credit Lyonnais 1.2 billion francs ($240 million), has long maintained the bank was at least partly responsible for the collapse of his business empire because it was involved in running it.

But the court delayed a final ruling on the liquidators' claim for a total 2.5 billion francs in damages and interest to await the outcome of another court case involving Tapie that involves an inquiry into bankrupcty proceedings at GBT and FIBT.
Credit Lyonnais would not comment on the court's decision. It has in the past strongly denied that it bears any responsibility for Tapie's troubles.

It no longer has any responsibility for SDBO and Clinvest. Under a massive state bailout of Credit Lyonnais last year, the two units were hived off from the bank and put under the ownership of state-backed rescue vehicle Consortium de Realisations.
The liquidators also ordered a three-man panel of experts to look into the sale of Adidas, the former flagship of GBT, which was sold off in 1994.

Tapie has accused Credit Lyonnais of forcing him to sell a majority stake in Adidas to a group of investors too cheaply and alleges the state-owned bank profited unfairly when it sold its holding in Adidas in 1994.
Tapie is hoping that the liquidators' case will establish that Credit Lyonnais owes him several billion francs from capital gains on the Adidas sale.
The bank has been battling to restore its profitability after a hectic lending spree in the late 1980s and early 1990s brought it to the brink of collapse.
Tapie's bankrupt status has forced him out of political life and obliged him to relinquish his French national assembly seat.
But the former socialist cabinet minister recently embarked on a film career, appearing as a lawyer in the Claude Lelouch comedy "Men, Women: Instructions for Use".
